intro.en: Temporary and lasting birth control asked in the practical exam: barriers, hormonal tablets, rings, patches, shots, implants, womb devices, emergency cover and sterilisation.

items.summary: A thin latex sheath worn over the erect organ as a barrier form of birth control, removed soon after climax and thrown away after a single act.

blocks.title: How to use it
bullets: Place it only when the organ is firm, unrolling it down to the base before any genital contact begins.
Pull out soon after climax, before softening sets in, holding the rim so nothing spills.
Peel it off away from the partner and use a fresh piece for every act.

blocks.title: Efficacy
blocks.text: About 98 in 100 users stay protected with faultless regular use. With everyday use the book quotes 15 to 18 pregnancies per 100 women years.

blocks.title: Advantages
bullets: Easy to use, cheap, and freely carried without a prescription or a clinic visit.

Guards against spread of sexually transmitted infections such as human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), human papillomavirus (HPV), herpes simplex virus (HSV), hepatitis B and C, gonorrhoea, chlamydia, syphilis and trichomoniasis.
Lowers the chance of pelvic inflammatory disease and causes no body-wide effects.
Gives cover after vasectomy while the couple waits for semen reports showing clearance.

blocks.title: Disadvantages
bullets: Success rests fully on the user, and ordinary use fails far more often than careful use.
Unsuitable with latex sensitivity, and a piece may split or slip off during the act.
A new pack is needed each time, and one may not be at hand when needed.
Some users feel it dulls pleasure during the act.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: People sensitive to latex can switch to sheaths made of polyurethane.

viva.q: How should a couple be taught to use the male sheath?
viva.a: Unroll to the base on the firm organ before contact, withdraw before softening, remove away from the partner, and use a new piece each time.

viva.q: Name two strengths of this method besides birth control.
viva.a: It blocks sexually transmitted infections and lowers pelvic inflammatory disease, with no body-wide effects.

viva.q: What option exists for a latex-sensitive user?
viva.a: A sheath made of polyurethane instead of latex.

image.brief: Single male latex sheath beside its foil pack on a plain light background, side view, rolled rim and teat end clearly seen, no people, no brand marks.

items.summary: A soft polyurethane pouch with two rings that lines the vagina, giving the woman a barrier she can fit herself before the act.

blocks.title: How to use it
bullets: Fit it before the act: the small closed inner ring sits up at the top of the vagina and the wide open outer ring stays at the entrance.
Check during the act that the outer ring has not slipped inside and that the organ stays within the pouch.
The book states the pouch can be washed and used more than once.

blocks.title: Efficacy
blocks.text: About 95 in 100 users stay protected with faultless regular use. With everyday use the book quotes 15 to 20 pregnancies per 100 women years.

blocks.title: Advantages
bullets: Guards against sexually transmitted infections such as HIV, HPV, HSV, hepatitis B and C, gonorrhoea, chlamydia, syphilis and trichomoniasis.
Lowers the chance of pelvic inflammatory disease and causes no body-wide effects.

blocks.title: Disadvantages
bullets: Success rests fully on the user, and ordinary use fails far more often than careful use.
The pouch may split or slip during the act, and some partners feel it dulls pleasure.
It costs more than the male sheath and the book notes that fitting may need trained help.

blocks.title: Related cervical barriers
bullets: Diaphragm: a latex or silicon dome barrier at the neck of the womb; place about 5 ml of spermicide in the dome, fit before the act, and leave it for 6 to 8 hours after. Keeping it beyond 24 hours risks toxic shock syndrome.
Cervical cap: a small cup that grips the neck of the womb snugly; fit before the act, leave for 6 to 8 hours after, and never keep it beyond 72 hours.

viva.q: Where do the two rings of the female pouch sit?
viva.a: The small closed ring rests at the top of the vagina and the wide open ring stays at the entrance.

viva.q: How long must a diaphragm and a cervical cap stay in?
viva.a: Both stay 6 to 8 hours after the act; the dome must come out within 24 hours and the cap within 72 hours.

viva.q: Why is keeping a diaphragm too long risky?
viva.a: Leaving it beyond 24 hours can trigger toxic shock syndrome.

image.brief: Single female polyurethane pouch on a plain light background, three-quarter view, small closed inner ring and wide open outer ring both labelled by position, no people.

items.summary: Daily steroidal tablets that pair an oestrogen with a progestogen, taken for three weeks followed by a one-week pause with dummy tablets.

blocks.title: What is in the tablet
blocks.text: Each tablet holds 30 micrograms of ethinyl estradiol with 150 micrograms of levonorgestrel. Sold as MALA-N, MALA-D, KRIMSON-35, YAZ, YASMIN, FEMILON and NOVELON.

blocks.title: When to start
blocks.text: Begin on days 1 to 5 of the cycle, then take one tablet daily at a fixed hour.

blocks.title: How it works
bullets: Its chief action is to stop the ovary from releasing an egg each cycle.
It changes the womb lining so a fertilised egg cannot settle.
Its progestogen thickens neck-of-womb mucus, barring sperm entry.
It also disturbs tube movement and transport of the fertilised egg.

blocks.title: Efficacy
blocks.text: About 99.7 in 100 users stay protected with faultless regular use, quoted as 0.3 pregnancies per 100 woman years.

blocks.title: Benefits beyond birth control
bullets: Eases acne, painful periods, mid-cycle pain, premenstrual syndrome and menopausal complaints, and steadies cycle timing.
Lessens monthly loss, so anaemia from heavy periods improves; also used in heavy bleeding, fibroids, endometriosis and excess hair.
Lowers pelvic inflammatory disease, ectopic gestation, ovarian cysts, benign breast lumps and iron-deficiency states.
Long use cuts ovarian and womb-lining cancer by about half over 15 years and bowel cancer by about 40 in 100.

blocks.title: Advantages
bullets: Strong cover that is unlinked to the act and leaves future fertility untouched.
Needs no clinic visits, unlike coil, implant or injection methods.

blocks.title: Disadvantages
bullets: Needs a tablet every day at the right hour, so drive and follow-through matter and poor compliance is common.
Costs more than barrier methods and interacts with liver enzyme inducers.
Can cause body-wide effects listed below.

blocks.title: Minor unwanted effects
bullets: Bleeding between periods, breakthrough spotting, nausea, vomiting, headache and breast pain.
Mood shifts and weight gain are often blamed on the pill but the book notes proof is lacking.

blocks.title: Major unwanted effects
bullets: Clots in leg or lung veins, raised blood pressure, heart attack and stroke.
Breast cancer risk is listed as a major concern with these tablets.

groups.label: Absolute bars
bullets: First 6 weeks after birth while breastfeeding; blood pressure 160 over 100 or higher.
Major surgery with long bed rest; being wheelchair bound is listed under relative cautions, not here.
Complicated valve disease, complicated birth defects of the heart, ischaemic heart disease, heart attack, weak heart muscle, or atrial fibrillation.
Vein clots, clotting tendency, migraine with aura, smoking above 15 cigarettes a day past age 35, or current breast cancer.
Liver adenoma, liver cancer, severe cirrhosis, lupus with antibodies, or antiphospholipid antibodies.

groups.label: Relative cautions
bullets: First 3 weeks after birth without breastfeeding; blood pressure 140 to 159 over 90 to 99.
Wheelchair immobility unrelated to surgery; diabetic kidney, eye or nerve damage; body mass index (BMI) above 35.
Smoking below age 35; migraine with aura that ended over 5 years back.
Breast cancer treated 5 years back, unexplained breast lump, acute hepatitis, gallbladder disease, or oestrogen-linked bile sludging in a past pregnancy.

head: Situation
What to tell her
rows: Swallow it the moment she recalls, even if that means two in one day, then finish the pack as usual.
Take only the most recently missed one, drop the earlier one, finish the pack, and add emergency cover if the couple met that week.
If the first 7 days were taken correctly, take the latest missed one, finish the pack, and use extra cover for 7 days if the couple met that week.
Take the latest missed one, finish the pack, skip the pause week and start a fresh pack at once (21 tablets straight after 21).

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: The national programme gives MALA-N free of cost; packs run 3 weeks of active tablets plus one week of iron dummy tablets.
Later-generation tablets cause fewer unwanted effects, but fourth-generation progestogens carry more vein-clot risk than second- and third-generation ones.
Yasmin pairs drospirenone with ethinylestradiol and counts as fourth generation.

viva.q: What is the standard strength of the combined tablet in this book?
viva.a: 30 micrograms ethinyl estradiol with 150 micrograms levonorgestrel.

viva.q: Name three absolute bars to prescribing it.
viva.a: Vein clots, migraine with aura, and blood pressure 160 over 100 or higher, among others.

viva.q: What should a woman do after missing two tablets in the third week?
viva.a: Take the latest missed one, finish the pack, skip the pause week and start a new pack at once.

viva.q: Why is the pill useful in heavy periods?
viva.a: It trims monthly loss, which lifts anaemia, and it is also used to treat heavy bleeding itself.

image.brief: Single 28-day combined pill strip on a plain light background, top view, three weeks of active tablets plus one week of dummy tablets visible in order, no brand pack.

items.summary: A soft combined-hormone ring worn inside the vagina for three weeks at a stretch, followed by one ring-free week.

blocks.title: What it holds
blocks.text: The ring pairs ethinylestradiol with etonogestrel, the same two-hormone logic as the combined tablet in a local form.

blocks.title: How to use it
bullets: Keep one ring in place for three full weeks without a break.
Then spend one week with no ring before starting the next cycle.
If the ring slips out, rinse and refit promptly and seek advice if it stayed out long.

blocks.title: How it works
bullets: Like other combined methods it chiefly holds back ovulation each cycle.
It also thickens neck-of-womb mucus and alters the womb lining against settling.

blocks.title: Counselling points
bullets: Stress the three-plus-one rhythm so the user never stretches the free week.
Explain that bleeding in the free week is expected and not a sign of failure.
Review clot warning signs and smoking risk as with any oestrogen method.

viva.q: Which two hormones does the combined ring hold?
viva.a: Ethinylestradiol with etonogestrel.

viva.q: What is the wear schedule?
viva.a: Three weeks with the ring in, then one week with no ring.

image.brief: Single translucent combined vaginal ring on a plain light background, three-quarter view, circular shape and even thickness clearly seen beside a coin for scale, no packaging.

items.summary: A combined-hormone skin patch changed once a week for three weeks, followed by one patch-free week.

blocks.title: What it holds
blocks.text: The patch pairs ethinylestradiol with norelgestromin, delivered steadily through the skin.

blocks.title: How to use it
bullets: Stick on one fresh patch each week for three weeks in a row.
Then spend one week with no patch before starting the next cycle.
Press each patch onto clean dry skin and check daily that its edges still cling.

blocks.title: How it works
bullets: Like other combined methods it chiefly holds back ovulation each cycle.
It also thickens neck-of-womb mucus and alters the womb lining against settling.

blocks.title: Counselling points
bullets: Stress the weekly change day so no patch stays on into the free week.
Explain that bleeding in the free week is expected and not a sign of failure.
Review clot warning signs and smoking risk as with any oestrogen method.

viva.q: Which two hormones does the Evra patch hold?
viva.a: Ethinylestradiol with norelgestromin.

viva.q: What is the patch schedule?
viva.a: One patch per week for three weeks, then one week with no patch.

image.brief: Single square combined skin patch on a plain light background, top view with a fingertip lifting one corner to show the thin adhesive layer, no brand marks.

items.summary: Daily tablets holding only a progestogen, taken at the same hour every day with no pause week, suited to users who must avoid oestrogen.

blocks.title: What is in the tablet
blocks.text: Brands named are MICRONOR and NORIDAY with norethisterone, NORGESTON with levonorgestrel, and CERAZETTE with desogestrel, each as a progestogen-only tablet.

blocks.title: When to start
blocks.text: Begin on days 1 to 5 of the cycle and swallow one tablet daily at the same hour through the whole month.

blocks.title: How it works
bullets: Thickens neck-of-womb mucus so sperm cannot swim through.
Changes the womb lining so a fertilised egg cannot settle.
Disturbs tube movement and transport of the fertilised egg.
Cerazette alone halts ovulation in about 98 in 100 cycles; other minipills do so in only about 60 in 100.

blocks.title: Efficacy
blocks.text: About 99 in 100 users stay protected with faultless regular use, quoted as near one pregnancy per 100 woman years.

blocks.title: Advantages
bullets: Free of oestrogen effects, so it suits breastfeeding mothers and users past 35 up to age 55.
Usable where oestrogen is barred, such as raised pressure, smoking, diabetes, obesity, vein clots and migraine without aura.
Unlinked to the act, leaves future fertility untouched, needs no clinic visits, and lowers pelvic inflammatory disease.

blocks.title: Disadvantages
bullets: Fails more often than the combined tablet and gives no shield against sexually transmitted infections.
Needs a tablet daily at the right hour, so drive and follow-through matter and poor compliance is common.
Costs more than barrier methods and loses strength with liver enzyme inducers.

blocks.title: Unwanted effects
bullets: Spotting between periods or no periods at all, breast pain, headache, acne and weight gain.

groups.label: Absolute bars
bullets: Current breast cancer, unexplained vaginal bleeding, ongoing pregnancy, or regular use of liver enzyme inducers.

groups.label: Relative cautions
bullets: Current ischaemic heart disease, stroke, migraine with aura, or past breast cancer.
Active viral hepatitis, liver tumour, unexplained vaginal bleeding work-up pending, or persistent molar-pregnancy disease.

blocks.title: Late or missed tablet advice
bullets: Classic minipills: if over 3 hours late (27 hours since the last tablet), swallow one at once, carry on as usual, and add extra cover for 48 hours.
Cerazette with desogestrel: the same steps apply once over 12 hours late (36 hours since the last tablet), with extra cover for 48 hours.
If she vomits within 2 hours of the dose, she should swallow another tablet.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Desogestrel in Cerazette is the one minipill progestogen that acts mainly by halting ovulation.
Unlike the combined pack there is no pause week: one tablet every day.

viva.q: Which minipill reliably halts ovulation, and how often?
viva.a: Cerazette with desogestrel, in about 98 in 100 cycles; others manage only about 60.

viva.q: Name two users for whom the minipill beats the combined pill.
viva.a: Breastfeeding mothers and anyone barred from oestrogen, such as smokers or those with raised pressure.

viva.q: What if she vomits within 2 hours of the dose?
viva.a: She should swallow another tablet and carry on with the pack.

image.brief: Single minipill strip of uniform tablets on a plain light background, top view, even daily sequence with weekday order visible, no brand pack.

unsure: Tablet strengths printed as 350 mg norethisterone, 30 mg levonorgestrel and 75 mg desogestrel look like microgram values mislabelled as mg, so doses were left out.

items.summary: A long-acting reversible progestogen shot given every few weeks, useful where daily tablets or clinic-heavy methods fail.

blocks.title: What is given
blocks.text: Two forms exist: depot medroxyprogesterone acetate (DMPA), sold as DEPO PROVERA or MYONE DEPOT, and norethisterone enanthate (NET-EN), sold as NORISTERAT or SYNGESTAL.

blocks.title: When to start
blocks.text: Give the first shot on days 1 to 5 of the cycle.

blocks.title: How it works
bullets: Its chief action is to stop the ovary from releasing an egg.
Thickens neck-of-womb mucus so sperm cannot swim through.
Changes the womb lining so a fertilised egg cannot settle.
Disturbs tube movement and transport of the fertilised egg.

blocks.title: Efficacy
blocks.text: About 99.9 in 100 users stay protected with faultless regular use, quoted as near 0.1 pregnancies per 100 woman years.

blocks.title: Dose and timing
bullets: DMPA is a water-based prefilled shot of 150 mg given once every 12 weeks; the commoner of the two.
NET-EN is an oil-based shot of 200 mg given once every 8 weeks, only into muscle, and is the less used one.
DMPA also comes as a 104 mg under-skin press called SAYANA PRESS, gentler in effects, patient friendly and self-given.
DMPA goes into muscle as Depo MPA or under the skin as Sayana Press.

blocks.title: Advantages
bullets: Safe, strongly effective, long acting, reversible, unlinked to the act, and unaffected by enzyme inducers.
Suits users with learning difficulties, migraine, or recent vasectomy waits, and fits the weeks after birth.
Needs no daily remembering, so follow-through is better, and it lowers pelvic inflammatory disease.

blocks.title: Disadvantages
bullets: Weight gain, absent periods, slow return of fertility, and no shield against sexually transmitted infections.
Bone mineral thinning when used beyond 2 years.

blocks.title: Benefits beyond birth control
bullets: Trims heavy-period loss and anaemia, eases period pain and endometriosis, and shields against womb-lining and ovarian cancer.
Cuts sickle-cell crises in affected users.

blocks.title: Unwanted effects
bullets: Headache, mood shifts, acne, weight gain and irregular spotting.

groups.label: Absolute bars
bullets: Current breast cancer.

groups.label: Relative cautions
bullets: Vessel disease, ischaemic heart disease, stroke, or past breast cancer.
Active viral hepatitis, liver tumours, persistent molar-pregnancy disease, or unexplained vaginal bleeding.

blocks.title: Late shot advice
bullets: DMPA overdue past 14 weeks: add extra cover for 7 days, with or without emergency tablets depending on whether the couple met after 14 weeks.
NET-EN overdue past 10 weeks: the same 7-day extra cover rule applies around the 10-week mark.

viva.q: Compare the timing of the two injectables.
viva.a: DMPA 150 mg every 12 weeks; NET-EN 200 mg every 8 weeks.

viva.q: What is Sayana Press?
viva.a: A 104 mg under-skin form of DMPA the user can give herself, with fewer effects.

viva.q: Name two drawbacks to warn about.
viva.a: Weight gain with slow return of fertility, and bone thinning beyond 2 years of use.

viva.q: What if DMPA runs past 14 weeks?
viva.a: Add extra cover for 7 days, plus emergency tablets if the couple met after 14 weeks.

image.brief: Single prefilled depot injection syringe with needle cap on beside its empty vial on a plain light background, side view, dose markings visible, no brand labels.

items.summary: A thin progestogen rod slipped under the skin of the arm that guards for 3 years, then is taken out and can be replaced.

blocks.title: What is fitted
blocks.text: A non-breakdown skin rod holding 68 mg of etonogestrel, sold as NEXPLANON; older rods were IMPLANON and NORPLANT. Jadelle and Sino implants are other examples, while Norplant is no longer used.

blocks.title: When and how it is fitted
bullets: Fit on days 1 to 5 of the cycle, under local numbing in the arm.
Place it 8 to 10 cm above the inner elbow bump, entering at 30 degrees to the skin then flattening once the needle tip passes the dermis.
Feel the rod after fitting to prove it sits in place.

blocks.title: How it works
bullets: Its chief action is to stop the ovary from releasing an egg.
Thickens neck-of-womb mucus so sperm cannot swim through.
Changes the womb lining so a fertilised egg cannot settle.
Disturbs tube movement and transport of the fertilised egg.

blocks.title: Efficacy
blocks.text: About 99.9 in 100 users stay protected with faultless regular use, quoted as near 0.1 pregnancies per 100 woman years.

blocks.title: Advantages
bullets: Safe, strongly effective, long acting, reversible and unlinked to the act, with better follow-through than daily tablets.
Unaffected by enzyme inducers and suits migraine, obesity and learning difficulties.
Trims heavy-period loss and anaemia and eases period pain.

blocks.title: Disadvantages
bullets: Needs a driven user plus trained hands for fitting and removal.
Gives no shield against sexually transmitted infections.

blocks.title: Unwanted and fitting effects
bullets: Spotting between periods or no periods at all.
Failed placement, deep placement, rod breakage, nerve or vessel nick, and scar tissue sealing the rod.

groups.label: Absolute bars
bullets: Breast cancer.

groups.label: Relative cautions
bullets: Vessel disease, ischaemic heart disease, stroke, or past breast cancer.
Active viral hepatitis, liver tumours, persistent molar-pregnancy disease, or unexplained vaginal bleeding.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: The rod carries a barium sulphate coat, so a lost rod shows on X-ray.
Lost rod drill: image with ultrasound or X-ray; if still unseen, test blood for etonogestrel. A level proves it sits inside and it can then be taken out; none means it left the body.

viva.q: What does the current implant hold and how long does it last?
viva.a: 68 mg of etonogestrel, guarding for 3 years.

viva.q: Where and at what angle is it fitted?
viva.a: 8 to 10 cm above the inner elbow, entering at 30 degrees then flattening, under local numbing.

viva.q: How is a lost rod traced?
viva.a: Image with ultrasound or X-ray, then blood etonogestrel: a level proves it is inside, none means it is gone.

image.brief: Single slender contraceptive rod beside its applicator on a plain light background, side view, applicator slider and grip area visible, inner arm marked for the fitting zone, no people.

unsure: Rod sizes printed near implant figures (4 cm, 3.4 cm, 4.3 cm lengths with mixed mm widths) were too garbled to trust, so dimensions were left out.

items.summary: A T-shaped copper device placed inside the womb that guards for 3 to 10 years, with no daily action and full return of fertility after removal.

blocks.title: When and how it is fitted
bullets: Fit between days 1 and 5 of the cycle in the outpatient room under full sterile care.
Gauge womb length with a uterine sound, set that length on the inserter guard, and pass the loaded inserter inside.
Hold the plunger steady while drawing the sleeve back (the withdrawal trick), so the arms open in place, then trim the threads.

blocks.title: How it works
bullets: Copper hampers sperm and egg so fertilisation fails.
Copper alters neck-of-womb mucus, barring sperm entry.
Mild sterile inflammation of the lining blocks settling of any fertilised egg.
Tube movement speeds up, further upsetting transport.

blocks.title: Efficacy
blocks.text: About 99 to 99.9 in 100 users stay protected with faultless regular use, quoted as 0.1 to 1 pregnancies per 100 woman years.

blocks.title: Advantages
bullets: Safe, strongly effective, long acting up to 10 years, reversible and unlinked to the act.
Unaffected by enzyme inducers, needs only brief training to fit, and causes no body-wide hormonal effects.
Suits migraine, obesity, raised pressure, diabetes, vessel and heart disorders, and learning difficulties.

blocks.title: Disadvantages
bullets: Needs a driven user and gives no shield against pelvic infection or sexually transmitted infections.
If it fails, any pregnancy is likelier to sit outside the womb.

blocks.title: Unwanted effects
bullets: Womb perforation, lower-abdominal pain, pelvic infection, expulsion, heavy period loss, fainting at fitting, or pregnancy with the device in place.

groups.label: Absolute bars
bullets: Ongoing pregnancy, recent birth or abortion with sepsis, or raised pregnancy-hormone levels in molar disease.
Unexplained vaginal bleeding, cancer of the cervix or lining, current pelvic infection, chlamydia, gonorrhoea, or pelvic tuberculosis.

groups.label: Relative cautions
bullets: Between 48 hours and 4 weeks after birth.
Womb cavity warped by fibroids or by a birth defect of the uterus.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: The digits on each device mark its copper surface in square mm.
The national programme gives Copper T 380 free of cost.
It also doubles as emergency cover (see the emergency item).
Expulsion peaks in the first 3 months; perforation runs near 2 per 1000 fittings and is commoner while breastfeeding.
Actinomyces-like organisms link to long-kept devices; Gynefix fits nulliparous users but slips out more often.

blocks.title: Lost threads drill
bullets: First exclude pregnancy, arrange backup cover, then image with X-ray or ultrasound.
Device inside the womb: lift out with a hook or hysteroscope. Device outside the womb: retrieve by laparoscopy.
No device seen means it has been expelled.

viva.q: How long do the common copper devices last?
viva.a: Copper T 380 A and T-Safe last 10 years, NOVA T, Multi Load 375 and Gynefix last 5, Multi Load 250 lasts 3.

viva.q: What do the digits on a copper device mean?
viva.a: They mark the copper surface area in square mm.

viva.q: Outline the lost-threads drill.
viva.a: Exclude pregnancy, arrange backup cover, image the pelvis; remove in-womb devices via hook or scope and out-of-womb ones by laparoscopy.

viva.q: When do expulsion and perforation cluster?
viva.a: Expulsion peaks in the first 3 months; perforation runs near 2 per 1000 fittings, commoner while breastfeeding.

image.brief: Single T-shaped copper device beside its inserter tube and plunger on a plain light background, top view, copper sleeves on the arms and stem plus trailing threads clearly seen.

items.summary: A T-shaped womb device that drips progestogen locally for 3 to 5 years, lightening periods while guarding against pregnancy.

blocks.title: When and how it is fitted
bullets: Fit between days 1 and 7 of the cycle, easing passage with local numbing or gentle widening of the inner opening.
Draw the threads into the inserter tube, lock them in the cleft at the shaft end, and pass the loader into the cavity.
Free the arms once the tip sits right, withdraw the loader, and trim the threads.

blocks.title: How it works
bullets: Alters neck-of-womb mucus so sperm cannot pass, and thins the lining within a month of fitting.
Mild sterile inflammation plus a foreign-body effect blocks settling of any fertilised egg.
Speeds tube movement; ovulation mostly carries on, with about 75 in 100 users still ovulating.

blocks.title: Efficacy
blocks.text: About 99 to 99.9 in 100 users stay protected with faultless regular use, quoted as 0.1 to 1 pregnancies per 100 woman years.

blocks.title: Advantages
bullets: Safe, reversible, strongly effective for up to 5 years, unlinked to the act, and usable while breastfeeding.
Suits migraine, obesity, raised pressure and diabetes, and helps users with learning difficulties.

blocks.title: Benefits beyond birth control
bullets: Trims heavy-period loss and anaemia, eases period pain and endometriosis or adenomyosis ache, and shields the lining against cancer.
Shields against pelvic infection and gives lining cover during oestrogen hormone therapy.

blocks.title: Disadvantages
bullets: Needs a driven user plus trained hands for fitting and removal.
Gives no shield against sexually transmitted infections, weakens with enzyme inducers, and any failure risks an extra-uterine pregnancy.

blocks.title: Unwanted effects
bullets: Womb perforation, lower-abdominal pain, pelvic infection, expulsion, fainting at fitting, or pregnancy with the system in place.
Acne, breast tenderness, irregular spotting, absent periods and ovarian cysts.

groups.label: Absolute bars
bullets: Ongoing pregnancy, recent birth or abortion with sepsis, or raised pregnancy-hormone levels in molar disease.
Unexplained vaginal bleeding, cancer of the cervix or lining, past breast cancer, current pelvic infection, chlamydia, gonorrhoea, or pelvic tuberculosis.

groups.label: Relative cautions
bullets: Between 48 hours and 4 weeks after birth; current breast cancer.
Womb cavity warped by fibroids or by a birth defect of the uterus.
Ischaemic heart disease, stroke, decompensated cirrhosis, or liver adenoma or cancer.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Mirena guards for 5 years as birth control but counts for 4 years as lining cover in hormone therapy, and frees about 20 micrograms of levonorgestrel.
Mirena and Jaydess both fit between days 1 and 7; unlike copper devices this system is not emergency cover.
Expulsion peaks in the first 3 months; perforation runs near 2 per 1000 fittings.

viva.q: How does the hormonal system differ from the copper device?
viva.a: It drips progestogen locally, thins the lining within a month, lightens periods, and mostly lets ovulation carry on.

viva.q: How long does Mirena last for each role?
viva.a: 5 years as birth control and 4 years as lining cover in hormone therapy.

viva.q: Name two absolute bars to fitting it.
viva.a: Ongoing pregnancy and current pelvic infection, among others.

viva.q: Can it serve as emergency cover?
viva.a: No; only the copper device doubles as emergency cover.

image.brief: Single T-shaped hormonal womb system beside its inserter on a plain light background, top view, hormone sleeve on the stem plus trailing threads clearly seen.

unsure: The book states Mirena frees 20 micrograms of levonorgestrel without a time unit, so no per-day rate was written.

items.summary: A keyhole sterilisation in which a tiny silastic band chokes a loop of tube until scar seals it shut.

blocks.title: What is used
blocks.text: A silastic ring band under half a cm wide, stretched over a narrow cone applicator at laparoscopy.

blocks.title: When to do it
blocks.text: Once pregnancy is ruled out, book it between days 1 and 5 of the cycle.

blocks.title: Steps
bullets: Draw a 2 to 3 cm loop of tube into the cone applicator at laparoscopy.
Release the stretched band onto the loop so it springs back and grips the tube.
Starved of blood, the gripped loop scars over and the healthy ends draw apart, sealing the passage.

blocks.title: How it works
blocks.text: Sealing both tubes bars sperm from meeting the egg, so fertilisation cannot occur.

blocks.title: Efficacy
blocks.text: About 99.9 in 100 users stay protected, quoted as near 0.1 pregnancies per 100 woman years.

blocks.title: Advantages
bullets: Daycare keyhole surgery with a quick procedure, small scars, little pain, brief stay and fast return to work.
Permanent, strongly effective, and quick for a trained surgeon to learn.

blocks.title: Disadvantages
bullets: Needs costly tools plus anaesthesia with its own hazards.
Risks bowel or bladder nicks and bleeding from nicked vessels.

blocks.title: Counselling points
bullets: Offer only to those sure their family is complete and who seek a lasting method.
Refuse or defer where keyhole surgery or anaesthesia is barred, and never proceed without the woman's own consent.

viva.q: How does the ring seal the tube?
viva.a: It chokes a 2 to 3 cm loop until blood loss turns it to scar, and the healthy ends draw apart.

viva.q: Name two strengths of the keyhole route.
viva.a: Daycare stay with small scars, and a quick return to work with little pain.

viva.q: When is consent alone a bar?
viva.a: Never proceed when the woman herself has not consented.

items.summary: Backup cover after unprotected intercourse using a progestogen tablet, a copper device, or an anti-progestogen tablet within strict hour limits.

head: Feature
Levonorgestrel
Copper IUCD
Ulipristal acetate
rows: 1.5 mg by mouth once (i-pill, E pills, Levonelle, After pill)
A 5-year or 10-year copper device (Cu-T 380A, Cu-T 275, Multisafe 375)
30 mg by mouth once (Ella One, Ella, Esmya)
Holds back or delays egg release, thickens neck mucus, checks follicle rupture and disturbs luteal phase
Copper poisons sperm and egg, bars fertilisation and settling
Holds back egg release, checks lead follicle growth and slows lining maturation

groups.label: Levonorgestrel
bullets: Sickness, vomiting, belly ache, painful periods, dizziness, altered bleeding and breast tenderness.

groups.label: Copper IUCD
bullets: Pain at fitting and the need for trained hands to place it.

groups.label: Ulipristal acetate
bullets: Headache, sickness, vomiting, belly ache, painful periods, dizziness and altered bleeding.

blocks.title: Who must not use each
bullets: Levonorgestrel: no bars listed in the book.
Copper device: ongoing pregnancy, unexplained vaginal bleeding, or active pelvic infection.
Ulipristal: severe liver disease, repeat use in the same cycle, pregnancy or breastfeeding, steroid therapy, or liver enzyme inducers.

blocks.title: Practical tips
bullets: Repeat the levonorgestrel dose if she vomits within 2 hours; double it to 3 mg with enzyme inducers.
Repeat ulipristal if she vomits within 3 hours, and pause breastfeeding for 36 hours after it.
Older backups: Yuzpe means 2 OVRAL tablets within 72 hours plus 2 more 12 hours later.
OVRAL holds 0.25 mg levonorgestrel with 50 micrograms ethinyl estradiol.
Further older backups: ethinyl estradiol 2.5 mg twice daily for 5 days, or mifepristone 100 or 200 mg once, each within 72 hours.

blocks.title: Trial and newer ideas
bullets: Gossypol, a cotton-plant male tablet, is unused since fertility does not return.
Spermicides such as nonoxynol-9 kill sperm and work best with domes, caps, sponges or sheaths.
RISUG: a kind synthetic fluid shot into each vas that bars and kills sperm at once.
Washing the fluid out restores flow, but study continues before routine use.
Intra-vas plug devices, hCG vaccines (hCG-TT, HSD-TT-DT, CTP-DT) that destroy post-fertilisation hCG, and anti-zona antibodies that bar sperm docking remain under study.

viva.q: Compare the hour limits of the three favoured options.
viva.a: Levonorgestrel within 72 hours; copper device and ulipristal within 120 hours, or 5 days.

viva.q: Which option doubles as routine cover?
viva.a: The copper device; the two tablets do not suit routine use.

viva.q: What if she vomits soon after the tablet?
viva.a: Repeat levonorgestrel within 2 hours, ulipristal within 3 hours; pause nursing 36 hours after ulipristal.

viva.q: Are any of the three abortifacients?
viva.a: No; none of the three ends an implanted pregnancy.

unsure: The RISUG diagram labels (styrene maleic anhydride coat, motile versus immotile sperm sketches) carried no extra facts beyond the text, so they were skipped.

items.summary: Lasting female birth control by cutting, tying or clipping both tubes, most often by a mini-open Pomeroy tie or by keyhole ring or clip.

blocks.title: Opening steps for the mini-open route
bullets: Work under full sterile care through a 2 to 3 cm cut: suprapubic, under the navel, or midline mini laparotomy.
Open the abdomen layer by layer, lift each tube with Babcock forceps and prove it by sighting its fringed end.

blocks.title: Modified Pomeroy technique
bullets: Loop the mid-isthmic segment up with the clamp and tie its base twice with 2-0 plain gut, keeping one thread long on forceps against retraction.
Open a blunt window in the fold beneath the loop, cut each limb apart leaving sound stumps, and send the piece for histology.
Check both cut faces for the tube opening and for bleeding, ease thread tension while watching, drop the tube back, and repeat across.

blocks.title: Parkland technique
bullets: A partial tube-removal method like Pomeroy except the fold window comes first.
Open the window in a blood-free patch under the loop, stretch it parallel to the tube, then tie a 2 cm mid-segment each side with separate 1-0 chromic.

blocks.title: Less used open techniques
bullets: Madlener: crush and tie a loop with lasting thread without cutting; the tied bit dies off but fistulae rejoin it, so failure runs high and it is unused.
Irving: at caesarean only, divide near the ampullary-isthmic joint, bury the near stump in womb muscle and the far stump between broad-ligament leaves, both sides.

Uchida: raise a saline-adrenaline bleb under the outer coat near the ampulla, slit the coat, strip it back, tie and cut the muscle tube, let the near stump sink beneath the coat, and purse-string the free far end.
Kroener fimbriectomy and Aldridge burial of the fringed end under broad-ligament peritoneum both fail too often for routine use.

blocks.title: Keyhole ring steps
bullets: Pass the band loader through a 10 mm operating scope or a 7 mm side port, with the band pre-stretched round the barrel.
Open the prongs inside, seat one each side under the isthmic tube in its fold about 3 cm from the womb corner.
Draw the prongs home so 1.5 to 2.5 cm of tube pulls in, let the band spring shut, and repeat across.

blocks.title: Keyhole clip steps
bullets: Trace the tube back to about 1 to 2 cm from the womb corner.
Open the Filshie clip in its applier, sweep it square across the tube until the lower jaw shows through the fold, proving full capture.
Squeeze gently but firmly to the stop, ease off, leave the clip seated, and repeat across.

blocks.title: Counselling points
bullets: Offer only to those sure their family is complete and who seek a lasting method.
Explain it is meant to be final; reversal fares worse than vasectomy reversal.
Mini-open success runs near 99.8 in 100 with about 2 failures per 1000.

viva.q: Which two female methods does the book call commonest?
viva.a: The modified Pomeroy tie and the keyhole Falope ring.

viva.q: How does Parkland differ from Pomeroy?
viva.a: The fold window is opened first, then a 2 cm mid-segment is tied each side with 1-0 chromic.

viva.q: Why are Madlener and fimbriectomy avoided?
viva.a: Their tied or cut segments rejoin through fistulae, so failure runs very high.

viva.q: Where is the Irving method done?
viva.a: At caesarean birth, burying the near stump in womb muscle; it is not an interval method.

image.brief: Diagram of both tubes after mini-open ligation on a plain background, front view, tied loops with trimmed stumps on each side of the womb clearly seen, no photograph of a patient.

items.summary: Lasting male birth control by cutting and tying each vas under local numbing, most neatly by the no-scalpel puncture method that needs no stitches.

blocks.title: How it works
blocks.text: Each vas ferries sperm into the semen stream; blocking both vasa bars fertilisation.

head: Point
Vasectomy
Tubectomy
rows: Pelvic pain or post-tie syndrome may follow

blocks.title: Conventional versus no-scalpel routes
bullets: Conventional: one midline or two side cuts with a blade, find each vas, cut and tie; the cuts are wide enough to need stitches.
No-scalpel: no blade and no stitches, through a puncture under 1 cm, with fewer tools and less cutting.

blocks.title: No-scalpel steps
bullets: Work under local numbing with full sterile care; pin each vas against the midline seam of the scrotum with ring forceps.
Nick the skin over the vas with fine mosquito forceps and stretch the nick to 1 cm at most.
Hook the vas out with a firm yet gentle grip, tie it twice, cut between the ties, and drop the sealed ends back.
Repeat across; the nick is too small for stitches, hence no incision means no stitches.

blocks.title: Aftercare
bullets: Painkillers, rest for a few hours, ice packs on and off for the first 8 hours, and scrotal support for 48 hours.
Resume routine in 48 hours and work by day 3; avoid intercourse for a week or until comfortable.
Use backup cover for 3 months until two semen reports show no sperm.

blocks.title: Strengths of the no-scalpel route
bullets: Shorter operating time with less pain, swelling and cutting, and faster return to work.
No blade, no cut and no stitches, yet failure matches the conventional route.

blocks.title: Complications
bullets: Bleeding, blood collection, infection, sperm granuloma, and epididymis inflammation.
Fear of pain, mind-driven impotence, worry over lost manliness, and a very rare urinary fistula from the vas.

viva.q: When does cover start after vasectomy?
viva.a: Only after 3 months, once two semen reports show no sperm; backup cover runs till then.

viva.q: Why does the no-scalpel wound need no stitches?
viva.a: The nick stays under 1 cm, so it seals on its own.

viva.q: How does success compare with tubectomy?
viva.a: Vasectomy nears 99.9 in 100 with 1 failure per 1000; tubectomy nears 99.8 with 2 per 1000.

viva.q: Name two complications to warn about.
viva.a: Blood collection in the scrotum and sperm granuloma, besides infection and bleeding.

image.brief: Diagram of the male tract after vasectomy on a plain background, side view, tied and cut vas sites marked on both sides with scrotum and testis in outline, no photograph of a patient.

items.summary: Lasting birth control by threading small coils into each tube through the neck of the womb, so scar tissue seals them over about 3 months.

blocks.title: What is placed
blocks.text: Bendable inserts of poly ethylene terephthalate fibres over a steel inner coil with a nickel titanium alloy outer coil.

blocks.title: Steps
bullets: Pass the insert through the cervix and womb into each tube under scope guidance.
The steel coil grips the wall and holds the insert in place.
Fibroblast growth into the coil over about 3 months chokes the tube shut.

blocks.title: Follow-up
bullets: Prove sealing with dye X-ray of the tubes before relying on it.
Use backup cover for the 3 months until sealing is proved.

blocks.title: Complications
bullets: Wrong placement, pain, infection, nickel allergy, or injury to the womb or tube.
Pregnancy with the inserts in place, including extra-uterine pregnancy.

viva.q: How long until the tubes seal after Essure?
viva.a: About 3 months, while fibroblast growth chokes the coils shut.

viva.q: How is sealing proved?
viva.a: With a dye X-ray of the tubes; backup cover runs until then.

viva.q: Name two complications to warn about.
viva.a: Wrong placement and nickel allergy, besides pain, infection or later pregnancy.

image.brief: Diagram of a coil insert seated in a fallopian tube on a plain background, cutaway view, inner steel coil and outer alloy coil with fibre mesh clearly seen at the tube opening.
